turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Morning. I'm just after checking you in. Blood pressure is 128 over 78, pulse is 88, temperature thirty seven point two. Grand, the doctor will be along.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Right. Is that, umm, normal? I don't know. Sorry, you're not the doctor.
[SEG0003] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): I'm the healthcare assistant. Those readings are fine. She'll call you in a minute.
[SEG0004] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hello, come on in, I'm Doctor Reilly. Tell me, what's brought you along today?
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): Eh, my eyes have gone yellow. And the pee is really dark. I'm wrecked, tired all the time.
[SEG0006] person_3 (DOCTOR): Ah, you poor thing. When did the yellow start, can you place it?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. Umm. Maybe a week? Could be five days. I can't pin the day down.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): And the dark urine and the tiredness, did they come on together?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, the pee went dark around the same time. The tiredness, well, actually I was already a bit flat on the trip, and then it got worse after I came home.
[SEG0010] person_3 (DOCTOR): Tell me a bit about the trip, whatever comes to mind.

[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Four of us, down the country for a long weekend. We were eating off those roadside stalls, burger vans and that. Two of the lads were throwing up the next day, and one fella said his eyes looked off as well. I don't know if it's the same thing.
[SEG0012] person_3 (DOCTOR): A few of you unwell after the vans. Ok.
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): The drive home was brutal though. The M50 was stopped dead, an hour sitting there, and the rain was lashing. You couldn't see the lights in front of you.

[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Then my brother is on about his new dog, a mad little collie that chewed the skirting the first night. He sent a video of the dog in a raincoat. We were in stitches in the car.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): A dog in a raincoat, I love that. Was the parking here any better this morning?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Worse. Three laps of the car park, and a jeep nipped into the space. Sure look, that's just how it is. Anyway.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right so, back to the urine. How dark?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Like tea. Dark tea. Not, err, not blood, just brown. I don't know, doctor, is that serious?
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): It fits with the yellow eyes. Any pain in the tummy at all?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No pain. Not that I've noticed, anyway.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): Have you been vomiting, or had a fever?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No vomiting. Fever, I don't know, doctor, I never took it. I felt warm one night but I couldn't say.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any itch in the skin? And the bowel motions, any change in colour?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): A bit itchy, yeah, the last few days. The toilet, I don't know, doctor, I didn't look. Sorry.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): Do you take a drink? Even on that weekend with the lads?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I don't drink. I never really have. They were on the pints, I was on tea.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): What about medicines, anything regular?

[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm, omeperazole, twenty milligrams, one in the morning, for the heartburn. That's years now. And if the head is at me I'll take two paracetamol, not every day, maybe once a week. I don't know exactly.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any reactions to drugs, antibiotics, painkillers, anything like that?

[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Penicillin. I'm allergic to it. I came out in a rash all over, and my lips swelled up. They said never take it again. That was years ago, but it's definite, I'm not mixed up on that.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): Good to know, we'll steer clear of penicillin and the amoxicillin family entirely. Had anyone checked your liver bloods before?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. About three years ago the GP said it was borderline. They never repeated it. I don't know the figures, doctor, they just said borderline.
[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): All right, I won't hang any decision on that old comment. Let me have a look.
[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): The whites of the eyes are yellow, and the skin has a yellow tinge. Tummy is soft. A little tenderness under the right ribs when I press, and no guarding.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm. So is it the liver? I don't know, doctor, I keep thinking the worst.

[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): My working impression is an acute hepatitis, quite possibly from that roadside food, seeing as the others were sick too. A blockage of the bile duct is still on the list, I can't rule it out properly until the bloods are back. Nothing is confirmed today.
[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): Here's what we'll do. Bloods Thursday morning at half eight, the liver tests and hepatitis serology, A, B and C. No fasting. The nurse will take them then.
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): If those liver tests come back borderline, then we do an ultrasound of the tummy. I'm not booking the scan now.

[SEG0039] person_3 (DOCTOR): Rest yourself, drink plenty of fluids, stay off alcohol, and keep the paracetamol to the odd dose only. If the yellow deepens or you start vomiting, don't wait for me, come back in.
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll see you here in two weeks with the results. That's a definite slot, not a maybe.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Right. I'll rest, plenty of fluids, no drink, and I'll go easy on the paracetamol. Thursday at half eight, no fasting. I don't know if work will moan, but I'll be there.
[SEG0042] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): I'll put the bloods in for Thursday at half eight, and the review in two weeks. No fasting, as Doctor Reilly said. You're all set.

spec.situation: Person with yellow eyes, dark urine and tiredness after eating at roadside stalls on a trip; others at the trip also ill; alcohol denied; liver blood tests and hepatitis serology planned.

traps.happens: The doctor asks about drug reactions. Variants (use ONE per encounter): (a) the patient says 'No, never, I have taken penicillin and everything' (no allergy); (b) the patient is unsure ('maybe the antibiotic or the painkiller, nobody told me which'); (c) a real allergy with the reaction described; (d) allergies are never asked.
traps.label_rule: (a) NO allergy entry: negative_findings 'Allergies' absent. (b) allergy with status uncertain, the substance as described, the reaction if said, plus an allergy_uncertain uncertainty. (c) allergy with the reaction. (d) nothing at all. NEVER list a medicine the patient has taken without a reaction as an allergy, and the plan must not prescribe a drug of a recorded allergy's family.

traps.happens: In the plan the doctor books some tests or visits for a definite time ('the nurse takes bloods Thursday morning', 'I'll see you in two weeks') and makes others conditional ('if those are borderline we do the third test', 'if it does not settle, a scan').
traps.label_rule: Booked or arranged = status planned. Only the hedged ones are conditional. Never mark a booked test conditional or 'if needed'. Instructions for the booked test (fasting, time, medicine timing) belong to that test's action, not a separate invented plan item.

features: test_result_recalled: the patient reports an old test or result ('they said it was borderline'); recorded as reported history/investigation only as far as said, not as a confirmed value.
tangent_small_talk: a long tangent or small talk (traffic, cricket, the weather, a grandchild) that holds NO clinical content; nothing from it is extracted.

omissions.text: Dark urine was described as 'like tea'/'dark tea', brown, and specifically not blood.
Fever was asked about; patient did not confirm fever, saying they never took their temperature and only felt warm one night.
Change in stool/bowel motion colour was asked about; patient was unsure because they had not looked.

History of possible infectious exposure: after eating from roadside stalls/burger vans on a long weekend, two companions were vomiting the next day and one companion said his eyes looked abnormal as well.
Prior liver blood tests were done by the GP about 3 years ago and were said to be 'borderline'; the recorded fact wrongly says they were requested by the patient.
Doctor advised specifically to come back urgently if the yellowing deepens or if vomiting starts, and not to wait.
Two-week follow-up was stated to be a definite booked slot, not tentative.
